summary: This short Informational document registers media types for Protocol Buffers, a common extensible mechanism for serializing structured data.

plainLanguage.summary: It gives official labels for a popular packing format, so computers can tell what is in the box.

subtitle: Official media type labels for serialized Protocol Buffer data

tldr.problem: Protocol Buffers, a popular method for serializing structured data, lacked official media type registrations, so people used non-standard labels like application/x-protobuf.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC registers two official media types with IANA: application/protobuf for binary Protocol Buffer data and application/protobuf+json for JSON-serialized Protocol Buffer data, along with optional parameters for encoding and version.
tldr.outcome: Applications can now reliably communicate the format of Protocol Buffer payloads using standard MIME type labels, improving interoperability and preventing content-type confusion.

today: RFC 9996 is an Informational RFC registering official IANA media types for Protocol Buffers. It has not been obsoleted and is the standard reference for labeling Protobuf-serialized data in transport and storage.

sections.title: What Protocol Buffers Are
sections.content:
Protocol Buffers (Protobuf) is a method developed by Google for serializing structured data—turning a complex object (like a person with a name, ID, and email) into a flat sequence of bytes that can be transmitted or stored, and then reconstructed into the original object. The Protobuf system includes three components: an interface definition language (IDL) for defining schemas, wire formats for encoding the data, and language-specific implementations in C++, Python, Java, Go, Swift, and many others.

Protobuf supports two wire formats: a binary format optimized for efficiency and a JSON format that represents the data as JSON. When serialized objects are transmitted over HTTP or stored in files, they need a media type label (also called a MIME type or content type) to tell receivers what format to expect. For decades, people used unofficial labels like application/x-protobuf; this RFC registers official types.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol Buffers is a system for packing objects into bytes in a compact way. Like a shipping box needs a label saying what's inside, protocol buffer data needs a label saying 'this is Protocol Buffer format'.

sections.title: The Two Wire Formats
sections.content:
The binary format encodes data as a compact sequence of bytes, optimized for network efficiency and storage size. Each field is encoded with a tag (a number identifying the field) and a wireformat (indicating the data type: int, string, bytes, etc.). This format is fast to serialize and deserialize but not human-readable.

The JSON format represents the same data as a JSON object, making it human-readable and easy to inspect with standard JSON tools. Both formats represent the same information; an application can choose either one depending on whether it prioritizes efficiency (binary) or readability/debuggability (JSON). The JSON format also makes it easier for web applications and JavaScript tools to work with the data.
sections.plainLanguage: Binary format is like a secret code—tiny and fast but nobody can read it without a decoder. JSON format is like English words—bigger but you can read it with any text editor.

sections.title: Official Media Type Registrations
sections.content:
The RFC registers two media types with IANA. application/protobuf is used for binary Protocol Buffer data. It has optional parameters: encoding (defaults to 'binary', indicating the binary wire format) and version (defaults to 1, indicating the wire format version, for future extensibility). Clients that receive data with encoding=json or an unsupported version MUST treat it as an error.

application/protobuf+json is used for JSON-serialized data and REQUIRES a charset parameter set to utf-8 (case-insensitive). It also supports optional encoding (defaults to 'json') and version parameters. The +json suffix indicates that the content is pure JSON, which helps browsers and security tools properly handle the data and prevent Cross-Origin Read Blocking attacks.

The RFC also notes that application/x-protobuf, application/x-protobuffer, and application/x-protobuf+json are deprecated aliases that some implementations may still use, but new applications should use the official types.
sections.plainLanguage: Binary Protocol Buffer data is labeled 'application/protobuf'. JSON Protocol Buffer data is labeled 'application/protobuf+json'. Both can have optional settings for which version of the format is being used.

sections.title: Schema Versions vs. Wire Format Versions
sections.content:
It is important to distinguish between the Protocol Buffer schema language version (Proto2, Proto3, Edition 2023, Edition 2024) and the wire format version. The schema language versions refer to the IDL syntax and features available when defining the schema. These evolve over time and bring semantic changes; for example, Proto3 handles unknown enumeration values differently than Proto2.

The wire format, however, has remained compatible across all schema versions. Any data serialized using any schema version will deserialize correctly with any other. Accordingly, the media type's version parameter refers only to the wire format version, not the schema language. The schema language can evolve independently. Future versions of the wire format may exist, but at the time of writing, all versions are wire format version 1.

Clients that receive a version parameter they do not understand MUST reject the payload.
sections.plainLanguage: The way you write the schema (how you define what fields a message has) has changed over time. But the way you encode it on the wire has stayed the same. If either one changes in the future, you label it with a version number.

sections.title: Security and Safe Handling
sections.content:
Protocol Buffers themselves contain no executable code; they are data. However, several considerations apply. Embedded content: A Protobuf message can contain string or bytes fields with embedded data (like a JSON string inside a string field). Applications must ensure the embedded format is exactly what they expect and validate UTF-8 encoding if applicable. Memory allocation: Malformed Protobuf data can be crafted to request allocation of huge amounts of memory, potentially causing denial of service. Implementations should limit memory allocation.

Web security: When sending binary Protobuf data over the web, servers should base64-encode it to prevent browsers from interpreting it as JavaScript or other executable formats. When sending JSON-serialized Protobuf (application/protobuf+json), the +json suffix ensures browsers treat it as pure data, preventing Cross-Site Script Inclusion and Cross-Origin Read Blocking attacks. Charset should always be specified for JSON encodings.

Protobuf provides no encryption, authentication, or integrity checking. Applications requiring these should use TLS for transport and application-level encryption and signing as needed.
sections.plainLanguage: Protocol Buffer data is just bytes, not code. But a broken message could freeze a computer by asking for too much memory. On the web, send binary data as base64 to keep browsers from trying to run it as code.
